notes:
I've written up notes on all 28 verses from what I could read. Three of your requests are only partly covered:

- **Traditions:** the sources I read mostly agree with each other. The only real split I found is between writers, not denominations, and it centres on verses 17–18, 24 and 26. I found nothing on Psalm 73 from the Methodist, Lutheran or Orthodox sites, from ag.org or pneumareview.com, or from netbible.org, so those are left out.
- **Pentecostal and charismatic:** David Guzik (enduringword.com) is the only teacher from your list in this group. I could only read his notes up to about verse 17.
- **Prosperity teaching:** I didn't find any prosperity or word-of-faith teacher writing on this psalm. Only their critics appear below.

---

**Introduction / title**
- Guzik says Asaph was the leading singer and musician of David's and Solomon's time, and a prophet in his songs. He divides the psalm by its main pronoun: "they" in verses 1–12, "I" in 13–17, "You" in 18–22, and "You and I" together in 23–28. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-73/
- Ellicott: the motive of this psalm shows itself clearly in Psalms 73:3—perplexity at the sight of the prosperity of the wicked. Two psalms have already dealt with the question at some length, viz., Psalms 37, 49. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html

**v. 1**
- **Usual reading:** the second line narrows the first, so "Israel" here means the true Israel. Ellicott thinks the very subject of the psalm seems to require a limitation here, and links it to Paul's saying that not all Israel is Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- The Cambridge Bible agrees: 'Israel' is thus defined as the true Israel of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/73-1.htm
- Gill (labelled Calvinist on StudyLight) reads "truly" as possibly "only". God is good to everyone in providence, but specially good only to his chosen. He adds that a clean heart is God's work, not something people can produce. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/73-1.html
- The Pulpit Commentary reads it as "in spite of appearances to the contrary". It mentions a suggestion that Absalom's rebellion shook Asaph's faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Matthew Henry says the psalm opens abruptly, as Asaph checks his own thoughts: "However it be, yet God is good." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_073.cfm
- Bible.org (Deffinbaugh) says verse 1 is both the introduction and the conclusion, showing where Asaph ends up. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-success-sinners-and-suffering-saints-psalm-73
- **Catholic/patristic (Augustine):** God is good to the right in heart. To the perverse he only *seems* perverse; God himself does not change. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801073.htm

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: "slipped" literally means "were poured out", a picture of weakness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says Asaph now sees his doubt as a sin. He had well nigh slipped from the rock of faith into the abyss of scepticism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Guzik quotes Boice: doubts like this can sit alongside responsible Christian living, because Asaph's feet only *almost* slipped. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-73/
- Augustine: he was about to stray but had not strayed, about to fall but had not fallen. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801073.htm

**v. 3**
- The Pulpit Commentary: to envy the wicked because they prosper is to make more account of the good things of this life than of God's favour - to prefer physical good to moral. It is also to doubt that God governs the universe by the strict rule of justice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/73-3.htm
- Barnes says the word is literally "the peace of the wicked." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/73-3.htm
- Guzik quotes Chappell: Asaph had been taught that the good always prosper, which made his problem worse. Guzik compares this to the beliefs of Job's friends and to John 9:2. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-73/
- Augustine says the peace Asaph envied was temporary and earthly, but yet such as I also was desiring of God. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801073.htm

**v. 4**
- **The translation is disputed.** Ellicott says the traditional wording fits poorly, and that a painless death for the wicked is out of keeping with the psalm. He thinks the text must be corrected and mentions a one-letter change: "no bands to their yoke", meaning they live without restraint. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- Gill gives the options: they die easily without pain, or "no bands until their death" (no troubles all their life). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/73-4.html
- The Pulpit Commentary compares Job 21:13. It says such deaths are a severe trial to anyone without a firm belief in a life to come. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Spurgeon (Treasury of David): however the verse is translated, it gives the psalmist's *mistaken* view, held before he went into the sanctuary. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-73.html
- Matthew Henry, quoted by Guzik: Men may die like lambs, and yet have their place with the goats. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_073.cfm
- **Augustine (Catholic) reads it very differently:** the wicked have peace now *because* their death is unavoidable and their punishment lasts forever. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801073.htm

**v. 5**
- The Pulpit Commentary sees some Eastern overstatement here. It adds that God often does not chasten the wicked because chastening would do them no good. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Treasury of David: their bread comes to them without care, their wine without stint. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-73.html

**v. 6**
- Ellicott says the necklace image may come from rich people's love of jewellery, or from calling the proud "stiff-necked". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- The Pulpit Commentary: because they are not afflicted, they think Heaven favours them. Their violence becomes like everyday clothing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Gill (quoted in Calvin's notes) says their clothes are often bought with what they took by violence. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom10/calcom10.viii.ii.html

**v. 7**
- The Pulpit Commentary pictures eyes bulging from fat faces. On "imaginations overflow" it says the exact meaning is doubtful. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Augustine contrasts the poor man who steals out of "leanness" with the rich man whose sin comes "out of fatness". https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801073.htm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: "they are corrupt" is an old rabbinic reading now abandoned. The sense is "they scoff", that is, they make a joke of sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- The Pulpit Commentary, following Cheyne: they talk of their oppressive plans as if they were gods speaking from heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm

**v. 9**
- Ellicott prefers "set their mouth *in* the heavens": pride boasting up to the sky and trumpeting itself around the world. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the split: some read it as blasphemy ("against"), while most modern critics read "in the heavens". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm

**v. 10**
- A hard verse. Guzik quotes Kidner: "Most modern versions find here the popular worship of success." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-73/
- Ellicott: the wicked win popularity, and people drink a full cup of flattery. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- The Pulpit Commentary: the wicked man draws followers into his ways, and they "drink iniquity like water". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- A sermon on Bible Hub mentions another view: "his people" are God's people, lured after the wicked by their glitter. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/73-17.htm

**v. 11**
- **Who is speaking?** Gill says the speakers admit God exists but doubt that he knows. If good people are speaking, they say it under temptation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/73-11.html
- Ellicott puts verses 11–14 in the mouth of the watching public, and has the poet then reject the idea himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/73-11.html
- Henry: some take verse 11 as tempted onlookers denying God's providence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_073.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary: Their wickedness breeds scepticism in them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm

**v. 12**
- The Pulpit Commentary compares Job 21:7–15. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Calvin says the complaint is that their prosperity lasts so long that it wears out the patience of the righteous. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_73
- Augustine: a fleshly soul would have sold its righteousness for visible things. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801073.htm

**v. 13**
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: Asaph questions the value of holiness when its wages are paid in the coin of affliction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-73/
- Henry: when the pure in heart see God (Matthew 5:8), they won't say they kept their hearts clean in vain. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_073.cfm
- Bible.org calls this Asaph's second confession: he began to see faith and obedience as wasted effort. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-success-sinners-and-suffering-saints-psalm-73

**v. 14**
- Guzik: "chastened" is worse than "plagued", because it suggests God himself was the one afflicting him. He adds that Asaph was overstating, as poets do. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-73/
- Augustine: Asaph's correction comes "in the morning", without delay, while the punishment of the ungodly is put off. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801073.htm

**v. 15**
- The Pulpit Commentary: speaking his thoughts aloud would have betrayed and tripped up God's people, so he kept silent, a reticence well worthy of imitation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Augustine: what held him back was Scripture's teaching that God cares about human affairs. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801073.htm

**v. 16**
- The Pulpit Commentary: he tried hard to work out God's ways, failed, and found the effort painful. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm

**v. 17**
- Ellicott: the temple service, with its readings of blessings and warnings, turned his thoughts to the consequences of sin. But he means consequences in *this* world, since belief in an afterlife was not yet firmly established. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- The Pulpit Commentary: the Hebrew is literally "sanctuaries". It compares Hezekiah taking Sennacherib's letter into the temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Guzik: in the sanctuary he met eternity. Prayer, worship and the word gave him understanding, not just feelings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-73/
- Desiring God says the sanctuary he entered was likely a place of sacrifice and blood. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/why-do-we-envy-the-wicked
- A Bible Hub sermon applies "sanctuary" to anywhere we meet God through his Word and prayer. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/73-17.htm

**v. 18**
- **This is where the commentators split.** The Pulpit Commentary lists historical downfalls of the wicked, such as Pharaoh and Jezebel. It says retribution after death "underlies the whole argument" even though the psalm doesn't say so outright. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Henry: if there were not another life after this, we could not fully reconcile the prosperity of the wicked with the justice of God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_073.cfm
- Ellicott thinks Asaph's answer here falls short of Psalm 49: the wicked simply stand on slippery ground. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: "in a moment" is literally "in a wink". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- The Pulpit Commentary notes how suddenly a wicked man's prosperity can collapse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm

**v. 20**
- The Pulpit Commentary: as a waking man despises his dreams, so God, when he rouses himself to judge, despises the mere "semblances" the wicked are. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Henry: no one envies a man the pleasure of a dream. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_073.cfm

**vv. 21–22**
- Ellicott: "grieved" is literally "soured", and "foolish" is better translated "brutish". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- The Pulpit Commentary, quoting Cheyne: "a pang of passionate discontent had pierced my inmost being". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Henry: the word is "Behemoth", a great beast. Beasts think only of the present. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_073.cfm
- Bible.org: Asaph's envy was "beastly". It was not God who was wrong but Asaph. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-success-sinners-and-suffering-saints-psalm-73

**v. 23**
- The Pulpit Commentary: he did not fall away, and God held him up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Gill (Calvinist) says the believer is kept and not allowed to depart from God "finally and totally". He distinguishes being always united to God from always enjoying communion with him. This is a Reformed perseverance emphasis, but I found no opposing view from another tradition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/73-23.htm
- Another commentator on the same page links "with thee" here to "a beast *with thee*" in verse 22: Asaph was foolish, yet still in God's favour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/73-23.htm

**v. 24 — the most debated verse**
- **Heaven after death:** Calvin reads the future tenses as God continuing to guide him until at length he received him into His glorious presence in heaven. Gill says "after death itself". Barnes says "receive me to thyself in heaven". https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/73-24.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says the psalmist "looks beyond this life", and notes that even the critic Cheyne sees Enoch's story "spiritualized" here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Coffman (labelled Arminian, Restoration Movement) calls it an Old Testament text promising resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/73-24.html
- **Honour in this life:** Ellicott prefers "with honour", following the Greek and Latin versions. The thought is not of a reward after death, but of that true honour which would have been lost by adopting the views of the worldly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- Bible.org (Utley's commentary) urges care not to assume NT revelation into ambiguous OT texts. There are OT texts that point toward a future hope of physical life with God. This text, however, may not be one of them. His reasons: "glory" never means heaven elsewhere in the Old Testament, it may mean "honour", and the verb is the one used of Enoch. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-73
- **Catholic translation:** the Douay-Rheims has with thy glory thou hast received me. Augustine reads God's leading as by Your gift, not by my work. https://biblehub.com/psalms/73-24.htm and https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801074.htm

**v. 25**
- The Pulpit Commentary: no angel or archangel can support him, only God. Earth offers even less. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Ellicott translates "Besides thee I have no delight on earth." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- One commentator on the Bible Hub page says that without God, heaven itself would be an empty waste. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/73-23.htm

**v. 26**
- "Strength" is literally "rock". God is the possession that can't be taken away (Cambridge, Barnes). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/73-26.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary quotes Cook calling this "A strong assertion of personal immortality". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm
- Benson: Asaph names the failure of both flesh and heart, but the remedy only for the heart, as if not caring about the body. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/73-26.htm

**v. 27**
- The Pulpit Commentary: being far from God, the source of life, is to perish. The psalmist is "vague" about the final fate of the wicked. "Unfaithful" (literally "go a-whoring") usually refers to idolatry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/73.htm

**v. 28**
- Ellicott: "works" means the truths revealed to the psalmist, not God's deeds. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-73.html
- Henry applies it as trusting God rather than any creature. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_073.cfm
- Bible.org: If "nearness to God" is our good, then whatever draws us to Him is good, and whatever draws us away from Him is not good. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-success-sinners-and-suffering-saints-psalm-73

---

**Prosperity teaching (as described by its critics)**
- Desiring God describes the wicked's mix of health, wealth and comfort as a prosperity "gospel" of degradation. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/why-do-we-envy-the-wicked
- Bible.org (Deffinbaugh) says studying this psalm deepened his warnings about the "prosperity gospel". He compares Asaph's early assumptions to the Pharisees, who took wealth as proof of piety. I don't find the saints being assured of peace and prosperity in this life. Rather, I find many indications that the saints will suffer. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-success-sinners-and-suffering-saints-psalm-73
- TGC Africa says God doesn't belittle his good gifts, but calls us to value his presence above any prosperity. https://africa.thegospelcoalition.org/article/psalm-73-learn-to-value-gods-presence-over-prosperity/
